issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat item about repeatedly checking doors and windows being locked implies a home-intrusion/external attack danger theme, which does not fit well with the illness-related threat pattern suggested by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
issues.explanation: Avoiding attention to one's own body is coherent for illness trauma, but it does not fit well with the selected threat theme of locking/checking doors and windows; together these items suggest incompatible danger models (internal bodily threat vs external intruder threat).

vignette: Ms. Leena is a 54-year-old South Eastern Asian woman who has recently sought help for symptoms related to her traumatic experience with life-threatening illness. Now divorced and working as an electrician, Ms. Leena's daily life is deeply impacted by the lingering effects of her trauma. One year ago, Ms. Leena was diagnosed with a severe form of pneumonia that nearly took her life. During her prolonged hospital stay, she experienced extreme physical distress and fear for her survival. The constant sound of heavy breathing from both herself and others in the ICU has become an auditory trigger that elicits intense anxiety whenever she hears similar sounds. The anniversary of the event is another potent trigger for Ms. Leena. Every year on this date, she finds herself reliving the traumatic experience, feeling as though it happened only yesterday. The overwhelming sense of helplessness and fear returns in full force, leaving her feeling overwhelmed and vulnerable. Ms. Leena also experiences strong reactions to hospital smells or antiseptic odors, which immediately transport her back to the ICU. These olfactory triggers are so powerful that they often lead to a dissociative response where she feels as though it happened to someone else. She has come to believe that this separation from reality helps her cope with the intensity of the memories. Whenever Ms. Leena encounters these triggers, whether through sounds at work or smells during routine medical check-ups, her body goes into an immediate state of alertness. Her muscles tense up, and she feels as though she is ready to react to any potential danger at a moment's notice. This heightened sense of threat makes it difficult for her to concentrate on her daily tasks and often leads to physical reactions like increased heart rate and sweating. The constant tension in her body and the feeling that it reacts before she can think about what's happening has become overwhelming. Ms. Leena is certain that these physical reactions are a sign that danger is always lurking, even when there is no real threat present. This belief further intensifies her avoidance behaviors, leading her to steer clear of hospitals and medical examinations altogether. When faced with reminders of the traumatic event, Ms. Leena often engages in counterfactual thinking, imagining how life would have been different if she had not fallen ill. These thoughts create a cycle where her fear and anxiety are perpetuated by both her avoidance behaviors and her heightened sense of threat. She is convinced that these strategies help her manage the overwhelming memories, but they only serve to reinforce her belief in the omnipresence of danger. In her current state, Ms. Leena feels increasingly isolated and disconnected from her work as an electrician. The fear of encountering triggers at her job site has led her to avoid certain projects or locations where there might be a higher chance of hearing heavy breathing sounds or smelling antiseptic odors. This avoidance has not only impacted her professional life but also strained her relationships with colleagues, who do not fully understand the depth of her struggles. What finally brought Ms. Leena to seek help was the realization that her daily functioning had been significantly compromised by these symptoms. She is most afraid of never being able to regain a sense of normalcy and safety in her life. At the same time, she hopes for relief from the constant state of alertness and physical reactivity so that she can return to living without constantly feeling as though danger lurks around every corner. In summary, Ms. Leena's trauma response is characterized by a complex interplay between triggers, maladaptive strategies, and heightened threat perception. Her efforts to dissociate and avoid medical cues have only served to reinforce her belief in the omnipresence of danger, creating a self-reinforcing cycle that she finds increasingly difficult to break.
